name: Diosmin

lead: Diosmin is a citrus flavonoid used to treat chronic venous insufficiency and haemorrhoids, usually with hesperidin. It is a prescription medicine in parts of Europe and a supplement in the US.
It is listed in bruise and swelling supplements; use for facial puffiness has not been tested.

paras: It is reported to raise venous tone, reduce capillary permeability and dampen leukocyte-driven inflammation after conversion to diosmetin.
Product labels mention mild stomach upset, nausea and rash, rarely bleeding or hypersensitivity. Combination bruise products carry additional warnings for their other ingredients.

label.generic: VITAMIN C, ZINC, ARNICA MONTANA EXTRACT, BROMELAIN, DIOSMIN, RUTIN, CITRUS BIOFLAVONOIDS, HESPERIDIN METHYL CHALCONE

lead: Diosmin is a flavonoid glycoside (diosmetin 7-O-rutinoside) found in citrus fruit and first isolated in 1925; it is made commercially by converting hesperidin from citrus peel. [1]

It is used as a venoactive agent for chronic venous insufficiency, haemorrhoids and leg swelling, often as a micronised purified flavonoid fraction of 90% diosmin and 10% hesperidin; in Europe products such as Daflon are prescription medicines, while in the US it is sold as a supplement. [1]

In looksmaxxing and appearance contexts it is of interest for swelling, puffiness and bruising. Bruise-support supplements list it alongside arnica, bromelain and vitamin C. [2] No trial located in the sources reviewed tests diosmin for facial puffiness or other cosmetic outcomes.
infobox: Prescription medicine in parts of Europe; supplement in the US

paras: The established use is symptomatic treatment of chronic venous disease. Grokipedia reports symptom improvements of up to about 50% in leg heaviness, pain and oedema over two to six months, a secondary and unverified statement. [1] Consumer bruise formulas containing diosmin state that they are intended to support recovery from bruising after minor injuries or surgery and list possible mild gastrointestinal upset, rash, and, rarely, prolonged bleeding or hypersensitivity. [2]

Diosmin is converted in the body to its aglycone diosmetin. It is reported to prolong noradrenaline-induced venous constriction, lower capillary permeability and reduce leukocyte adhesion, with antioxidant effects. [1] Laboratory work shows citrus flavonoids act on blood and endothelial cells, and a 2003 screen examined diosmin and other flavonoids at the aryl hydrocarbon receptor. [3][4]
Animal studies have reported protection against ethanol-induced gastric injury and chemoprevention of experimental colon carcinogenesis by diosmin and hesperidin. [5][6]

A 120-person phase 4 trial compared diosmin alone with diosmin plus hesperidin in symptomatic chronic venous insufficiency. [7] Other registered trials examine diosmin or diosmin-hesperidin in ovarian hyperstimulation prevention, ulcerative colitis, fatty liver disease, peptic ulcer, chemotherapy-related bone pain and neuropathy, and post-surgical seroma. [8][9][10][11][12] No studies found on facial puffiness, under-eye swelling or other cosmetic uses.

timeline.event: Diosmin first isolated from Scrophularia nodosa. [1]
